content.text: Both sectional briefs now direct differentiated hatching, and both remain within the 2800-character limit (FIG. 2 at 2790, FIG. 4 at 2787).

input.summary: Fixed the drawing-formality finding on the two sectional sheets. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 now specify regularly spaced oblique parallel hatching whose angle differs between each pair of adjoining bodies, so the boundaries between the base, the perimeter member legs and the covering element in FIG. 2, and between the covering element, bonding material, substrate and column in FIG. 4, read plainly rather than merging into one hatched mass. To hold both briefs inside the 2800-character limit while adding the hatching requirement, I removed generic rendering controls (the lettering recitals and a residual negative control) and some duplicated phrasing. No draft/ section, claim, numeral entry, or disclosed relationship was changed, and the numeral-to-sheet assignments are untouched.
reasoning: The finding is a 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) formality: juxtaposed different elements must be hatched at different angles. Both section briefs called every cut body simply 'hatched', and the parts they show are in direct contact, so the fix was to specify differing hatch angles between touching bodies. I used the reviewer's wording in both files.

FIG. 4 was the worse case because three different materials are stacked in contact, each pair meeting along a single shared line, with nothing but that line to separate them. The added clause ties the angle difference to the band each body touches and to the column, so no pair of adjoining bodies can share an angle.

FIG. 2 needed the same treatment for the slab, the two cut legs of the perimeter member and the covering element band, since the legs hang from the slab underside and stand on the band with no gap. The housing already stands outside the cut and is unhatched, so it needs no angle of its own.

Both briefs were close to the 2800-character ceiling before the addition, so something had to come out. I removed the recitals about which characters appear on the sheet and the view legend: the pipeline adds numerals, legends and leaders deterministically, so a brief asking the geometry image about lettering is a generic renderer control rather than invention geometry. Each brief now says only that no lettering is drawn.

I also dropped two residual negative controls, 'that broken line being all that is drawn for it' in FIG. 2 and 'Nothing else is drawn above the bands' in FIG. 4. Both are generic bans, and each is already covered positively: the opening sentence of each brief enumerates every body drawn and says nothing else appears.

The remaining trims are duplications, not substance: the housing's position on the slab, the legs standing on the band, and 'cut twice by the section' were each stated twice in the same brief. Every physical relationship the sheets must show survives, including the legs meeting the band along a common line with no gap and the column standing plainly apart from the uppermost band, which is what makes clearance 34 visible.

Endpoint targets were left alone. They are already broad interiors ('well inside its hatching', 'well inside that space') or the specific edge-on lines that identify bearing face 26 and exposed face 38, which cannot be broadened without pointing at the wrong part. Repeated bands are named as uppermost, middle and lowest and the cut legs as right-hand, so no ordinal can be read in two directions.

Nothing in draft/ changed. The hatching angle is a drawing convention for distinguishing bodies in section; it asserts no material, proportion or structure, so the claims, description, numeral table and Brief Description all stand as filed and stay synchronized with the briefs.
changes: figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: the three bands now carry regularly spaced oblique parallel hatching, each band's hatching angled differently from that of the band it touches and from that of the column, so the boundary between adjoining bodies reads plainly.
figures/FIG-4-...md: view line now states that no lettering is drawn, replacing the recital of which characters appear on the sheet and where the view legend sits.

figures/FIG-4-...md: the column description is condensed to one sentence describing it rising from the horizontal line closing it below to just inside the upper limit of the drawing area, hatched throughout between its two straight side lines; the generic 'Nothing else is drawn above the bands' control is removed.

figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: added the requirement that the base 12, the two legs of the perimeter member 24 and the covering element 36 each carry regularly spaced oblique parallel hatching, angled differently from that of the bodies each touches.
figures/FIG-2-...md: view line now states that no lettering is drawn, replacing the character and view-legend recital.

figures/FIG-2-...md: removed the negative control on the broken line and the duplicated statements that the housing stands on the slab, that both legs stand on the band, and that the loop is cut 'by the section'; condensed the first side 14 and chamber 22 endpoint phrasing without changing either target.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the edits are drawing conventions only. Claim 1 still rests on the combination absent from every reference in prior_art/: a rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately does not seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously; an extraction rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the differential is maintained. The rigid, seal-free perimeter carries the claim clear of US-11408462-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1, both of which place a compliant member, elastic partitions or a rubber-elastic apron, in the load path. Simultaneous holding and sliding under one continuously running extraction carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, which gives up the vacuum and floats on an air cushion to move. The non-sealing clearance, and vibration delivered into the covering element as the working output rather than spent loosening the hold, carry it clear of US-4934475-A. US-11247858-B2 is addressed in the Background for what it teaches, lifting sheet articles on a perforated suction plate and sweeping debris by suction, and why that does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a laid covering element.
input.answer: The sectional hatching defect is fixed in both places it was found. In figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md the three stacked bands, covering element 36, bonding material 40 and substrate 42, now carry regularly spaced oblique parallel hatching whose angle differs from that of the band each one touches and from that of the perimeter member column, so each shared horizontal boundary reads as a boundary. In figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md the base 12, the two cut legs of the perimeter member 24 and the covering element 36 are each specified with oblique parallel hatching angled differently from the bodies they touch, which matters because the legs hang from the slab underside and stand on the band with no gap. Both briefs had to lose some length to take the addition without breaching the 2800-character limit; they now stand at 2790 and 2787. What I removed was generic renderer control rather than geometry: the recitals about which characters and legends appear on the sheet, the ban on drawing anything for the fluid communication beyond the broken line, the ban on anything above the bands, and phrases repeating relationships already stated. Every required body, contact, opening and path survives, including the legs meeting the covering element along a common line with no gap and the column standing plainly apart from the uppermost band so that clearance 34 is visible. No file in draft/ was touched: the claims, detailed description, Brief Description of the Drawings, and the 16-entry numeral table are unchanged, and each sheet still carries the same numerals it did before, six on FIG. 2 and seven on FIG. 4.

structured_output.summary: Fixed the drawing-formality finding on the two sectional sheets. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 now specify regularly spaced oblique parallel hatching whose angle differs between each pair of adjoining bodies, so the boundaries between the base, the perimeter member legs and the covering element in FIG. 2, and between the covering element, bonding material, substrate and column in FIG. 4, read plainly rather than merging into one hatched mass. To hold both briefs inside the 2800-character limit while adding the hatching requirement, I removed generic rendering controls (the lettering recitals and a residual negative control) and some duplicated phrasing. No draft/ section, claim, numeral entry, or disclosed relationship was changed, and the numeral-to-sheet assignments are untouched.
reasoning: The finding is a 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) formality: juxtaposed different elements must be hatched at different angles. Both section briefs called every cut body simply 'hatched', and the parts they show are in direct contact, so the fix was to specify differing hatch angles between touching bodies. I used the reviewer's wording in both files.

FIG. 4 was the worse case because three different materials are stacked in contact, each pair meeting along a single shared line, with nothing but that line to separate them. The added clause ties the angle difference to the band each body touches and to the column, so no pair of adjoining bodies can share an angle.

FIG. 2 needed the same treatment for the slab, the two cut legs of the perimeter member and the covering element band, since the legs hang from the slab underside and stand on the band with no gap. The housing already stands outside the cut and is unhatched, so it needs no angle of its own.

Both briefs were close to the 2800-character ceiling before the addition, so something had to come out. I removed the recitals about which characters appear on the sheet and the view legend: the pipeline adds numerals, legends and leaders deterministically, so a brief asking the geometry image about lettering is a generic renderer control rather than invention geometry. Each brief now says only that no lettering is drawn.

I also dropped two residual negative controls, 'that broken line being all that is drawn for it' in FIG. 2 and 'Nothing else is drawn above the bands' in FIG. 4. Both are generic bans, and each is already covered positively: the opening sentence of each brief enumerates every body drawn and says nothing else appears.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
44	
45	The vibration transmission path
46	
47	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
48	
49	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
50	
51	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
52	
53	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
54	
55	Handles
56	
57	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
58	
59	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
60	
61	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
62	
63	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
64	
65	Method of use
66	
67	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
68

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

input.summary: Re-ran the failing check, source fidelity before rendering, over draft/01 through draft/10, draft/numerals.md and all five figure briefs. The application text traces to the disclosure and needed no change. The defects I found and fixed were all in the figure briefs: three sheets still carried the old lettering recital that the other two had lost, leaving the set inconsistent about what the geometry image draws; FIG. 3 prescribed a corner shape as a rendering control; and two endpoint targets carried modifiers narrower than needed to identify their part. All five briefs now use one lettering convention, the invented corner-shape constraint is gone, and the two endpoints are broad interiors. Every brief is under 2800 characters, numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged, and no draft/ file was touched.
reasoning: The failing mechanical check was source fidelity before rendering, so I rebuilt the trace myself: the rigid base and its two opposed sides, motor and air-extraction mechanism on the first side, chamber on the second, the rigid low-friction perimeter member in plastic, metal, PTFE or combinations of rigid materials terminating in a bearing face, the deliberate non-seal with continuous ingress through a clearance along at least part of the member, the extraction rate that holds the chamber sub-atmospheric under that ingress, the holding force that takes the operator out of the load path, the all-rigid path free of elastomeric, foam and resilient members, sliding while the differential is maintained, the guiding handle, and the flexible pulling element with decoupled control. Each traces to an affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md, so I changed no application text.

Across the last two turns I had replaced the lettering recital in FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 but not in FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5, which left three sheets telling the geometry image that numerals, leaders and a view legend appear on it. The pipeline adds those deterministically, so the recital is both a generic renderer control and inaccurate about what the image contains. All five now read 'No lettering is drawn.'

FIG. 3 required 'plain square corners' on both rectangles of the plan ring. Corner shape is exactly the kind of invented rendering constraint that has no source in the disclosure; the loop's plan outline is already declared a depiction convention. I removed the corner-shape clause and kept the positive statement that the band carries round each corner as one continuous surface, which is what makes the ring read as one closed body.

Two endpoints were narrower than they needed to be. In FIG. 1, device 10 was pinned to the corner line 'at the level of the joint between the slab and the band beneath it'; the level modifier is not disclosure-grounded and is unnecessary, because any point on the upright outer corner line already lies on the machine's silhouette rather than inside base 12 or perimeter member 24. In FIG. 3, perimeter member 24 was targeted 'deep inside that band, on a straight stretch away from the corners, with clear space on both sides before either edge': that is now simply well inside the band on a straight stretch, a broad interior target on the only body drawn.

I kept the two 'no attachment formation shown' clauses in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. They are not linework bans suppressing an artifact; they are source-fidelity guards against depicting a mounting structure the disclosure never describes, and the Brief Description now declares the FIG. 5 connection schematic, so the convention stays inside the drawing layer.

I also kept the FIG. 1 statement that the ring-shaped grip's bar has its own width. That is positive geometry, and the handle 44 endpoint depends on it: without a bar of some width the numeral would have nowhere on the part to land.

Trimming freed room rather than costing it. FIG. 1 fell to 2614, FIG. 3 to 1889 and FIG. 5 to 2598, with FIG. 2 at 2790 and FIG. 4 at 2787, so every brief sits inside the limit with the differentiated section hatching retained.

Nothing in draft/ moved, so the claims, detailed description, Brief Description of the Drawings and the 16-entry numeral table remain synchronized with the briefs; each sheet carries the same numerals as before, at most seven on any one sheet, and all 16 numerals remain covered.

figures/FIG-1-...md: the vibration device 10 endpoint no longer requires the level of the joint between the slab and the band; it is identified on the upright outer corner line at the front left, on the machine's outer silhouette.
figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: view line now states that no lettering is drawn, replacing the duplicated line-work and character recital.

figures/FIG-3-...md: removed the requirement that the corners of both rectangles be plain square corners, keeping the positive statement that the band carries round each corner as one continuous surface.

figures/FIG-3-...md: the perimeter member 24 endpoint is now a broad interior target, well inside the band on a straight stretch of it, without the clear-space-on-both-sides and away-from-the-corners modifiers.
figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: view line now states that no lettering is drawn, replacing the recital of characters, leaders and view legend.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged; this turn touched only figure briefs. Claim 1 continues to rest on the combination no reference in prior_art/ discloses: a rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately does not seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously; an extraction rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the differential is maintained. The rigid, seal-free perimeter carries the claim clear of US-11408462-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1, which both place a compliant member, elastic partitions or a rubber-elastic apron, in the load path. Simultaneous holding and sliding under one continuously running extraction carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, which surrenders the vacuum and floats on an air cushion to move. The non-sealing clearance, and vibration delivered into the covering element as the working output rather than spent loosening the hold, carry it clear of US-4934475-A. US-11247858-B2 is addressed in the Background for the teaching it actually contains, lifting sheet articles on a perforated suction plate and sweeping debris by suction, and why that does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a laid covering element.
input.answer: I re-ran the source-fidelity trace named in the failing check and then corrected what it turned up. Every limitation in claims 1-18, every one of the 16 numerals, and every relationship, material, result and operating condition in the specification traces to an affirmative passage in the inventor's disclosure, so no application text changed: draft/01 through draft/10 and draft/numerals.md are byte-identical to the version reviewed. The defects were in the drawing layer. Three briefs, FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5, still carried the old recital telling the geometry image which characters and view legend appear on the sheet, while FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 had been changed to say no lettering is drawn; all five now use the same convention, which is also the accurate one, since numerals, leaders and legends are added deterministically after the geometry. FIG. 3 prescribed plain square corners on both rectangles of the plan ring, an invented corner-shape constraint with no source in the disclosure; that is removed, and the positive requirement that the band carry round each corner as one continuous surface remains, so the ring still reads as one closed body. Two endpoints were tightened more than identification required and are now broad: vibration device 10 in FIG. 1 sits anywhere on the upright outer corner line at the front left, which is on the machine's silhouette and so cannot be mistaken for base 12 or perimeter member 24, and perimeter member 24 in FIG. 3 sits well inside the band on a straight stretch. The differentiated section hatching added for FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 is retained. Brief lengths are now 2614, 2790, 1889, 2787 and 2598 characters, all inside the limit, each sheet carries at most seven unique numerals, and the five sheets together still cover all 16 numerals with the Brief Description of the Drawings matching them one for one.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only; the only characters on the sheet are the listed numerals and their leaders, with the view legend FIG. 1 below the drawing.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, leaving a wide open expanse of tile to the right.

The machine is a plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Two plain closed housings stand on the top face of the slab, one left and one right, and a grip stands above the slab between them. Slab, band, housings, grip and tile are shown schematically, the plain rectangular forms being a depiction convention for this sheet only.

Each housing hides the part of the slab top face beneath it, and that face is seen between the housings and around the grip. The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile's upper face with no gap, and the machine hides the stretch of tile behind it.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the slab with its band, housings and grip. Identified on the outer silhouette of the machine at the front left, on the upright outer corner line at which the left-hand surfaces of the machine meet its front surfaces, at the level of the joint between the slab and the band beneath it, so that the endpoint lies on the boundary of the machine as a whole and not within any one of its parts.

input.summary: Fixed the duplicated line-work instruction in the FIG. 3 View line and brought all five View lines to a single parallel statement. The workspace had reverted FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 to an earlier state, so I also re-applied the drawing repairs that had been lost from those three sheets: the invented square-corner constraint in FIG. 3, the over-narrow endpoint targets for perimeter member 24 in FIG. 3 and vibration device 10 in FIG. 1. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 kept their differentiated section hatching, and both draft/ edits from earlier turns are intact. Every brief is under 2800 characters, numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged, and no draft/ file was modified this turn.
reasoning: The reported defect was in the FIG. 3 View line, which read 'Outline line work only. Line work only; the only characters on the sheet are the listed numerals and their leaders, with the view legend FIG. 3 below the drawing, clear of all line work.' That is the restriction stated twice in succession. It now reads once: 'Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.'

I did not restore the characters-and-legend recital that the parallel briefs used, because the pipeline adds numerals, leaders and the FIG. legend deterministically after the geometry is drawn. A brief that tells the geometry image which characters appear on the sheet is a generic renderer control and is also inaccurate about what that image contains. Saying no lettering is drawn states the same restriction once and unambiguously.

To remove any chance of the check reading two overlapping statements again, I made all five View lines parallel in the same single-sentence form: outline line work only with no lettering drawn for FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5, and line work with hatching on cut material and no lettering drawn for the two sectional sheets, which do carry hatching and so cannot say outline only.

On reading the files I found FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 had reverted to an earlier state, losing repairs made in an earlier turn. I re-applied them rather than leaving known defects standing: FIG. 3 no longer prescribes plain square corners on both rectangles, which is an invented corner-shape constraint with no source in the disclosure, and it keeps the positive statement that the band carries round each corner as one continuous surface so the ring still reads as one closed body.

Two endpoints were re-broadened. Perimeter member 24 in FIG. 3 is now identified well inside the band on a straight stretch of it, dropping the away-from-the-corners and clear-space-on-both-sides modifiers. Vibration device 10 in FIG. 1 is identified on the upright outer corner line at the front left without the level-of-the-joint modifier; any point on that corner line already lies on the machine's silhouette and so cannot be mistaken for base 12 or perimeter member 24.

I verified the two sectional sheets still carry the 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) hatching differentiation added earlier, and that both earlier draft/ repairs survived: the FIG. 5 sentence in the Brief Description still recites the flexible pulling element and its connection as shown schematically, and the description still says the second side 16 is opposite the first side 14.

Rewording the FIG. 2 View line pushed that brief to 2807 characters, so I trimmed two redundancies in it: 'single' before 'closed loop' in the perimeter member bullet, where the geometry paragraph already says one closed loop cut twice, and a conjunction in the housing sentence. FIG. 2 is now 2797, and the five briefs stand at 2616, 2797, 1891, 2792 and 2600.

No draft/ file changed this turn, so the claims, detailed description, Brief Description of the Drawings and the 16-entry numeral table remain synchronized with the briefs; sheet loads are still 7, 6, 2, 7 and 4, covering all 16 numerals.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged; this turn touched only figure briefs. Claim 1 still rests on the combination no reference in prior_art/ discloses: a rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately does not seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously; an extraction rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the differential is maintained. The rigid, seal-free perimeter carries the claim clear of US-11408462-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1, which both place a compliant member, elastic partitions or a rubber-elastic apron, in the load path. Simultaneous holding and sliding under one continuously running extraction carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, which surrenders the vacuum and floats on an air cushion to move. The non-sealing clearance, and vibration delivered into the covering element as the working output rather than spent loosening the hold, carry it clear of US-4934475-A. US-11247858-B2 is addressed in the Background for the teaching it actually contains, lifting sheet articles on a perforated suction plate and sweeping debris by suction, and why that does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a laid covering element.

input.summary: Repaired all five failing sheets in the figure briefs. The two sectional sheets rendered every cut body at one hatch angle because the briefs only asked, in the abstract, for adjoining bodies to differ; each body is now given an explicit hatch direction, so no touching pair can share one. The endpoint failures for numeral 24 on FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 came from a target region the renderer drew too thin to hit, so the perimeter member's visible surface is now specified as a broad strip or band with its bounding neighbours named, and the target sits inside it clear of both boundaries. Numeral 36 on FIG. 5 was aimed at the same open expanse of tile the pulling element sags across; it now targets the open stretch of tile in front of the machine, which the cord is required to stay clear of. All five briefs remain at or under 2800 characters, the numeral table and numeral-to-sheet assignments are unchanged, and no draft/ file was modified.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 failures were reported as identical hatching angles across bodies. The previous briefs stated the requirement as a relationship ('angled differently from that of the bodies it touches'), which the renderer satisfied by drawing everything the same. Relationships of that kind are not actionable by an image model, so each body now carries a stated direction: in FIG. 2 the base 12 rises to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs of the perimeter member 24 fall to the right at about 45 degrees, and the covering element 36 rises to the right at a shallow slope; in FIG. 4 the covering element 36 rises at about 45, the bonding material 40 falls at about 45, the substrate 42 rises shallowly, and the column falls shallowly.

Hatch angle asserts nothing about the invention. It is the 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) convention for showing that adjoining bodies are different elements, so specifying it adds no structure, material, or proportion to the disclosure, and the claims and description remain untouched.

The numeral 24 failures on three sheets share one cause: on FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 the perimeter member is drawn as a band beneath the slab, and if the renderer gives that band almost no depth there is no interior for the endpoint to occupy, so the marked point lands on the slab or the tile and is rejected. The briefs now state that the band's front surface reads as a broad strip standing between the underside of the slab or body and the tile, with the depth declared schematic and no proportion asserted, and the target is inside that strip clear of both named boundaries.

On FIG. 3 the same numeral failed against the plan ring. The band is now required to be drawn broad with its outer and inner edges standing well apart, and the target is inside the band on the straight left-hand side of the ring, clear of both edges and expressly not in the open field the ring encloses, which is the region belonging to second side 16. Left-hand is a stable position term, so the direction cannot be read two ways.

Numeral 36 on FIG. 5 was failing for a different reason: its target was the open expanse of tile to the left, and that is exactly where the flexible pulling element sags. The brief now establishes an open stretch of tile in front of the machine down to the near edge of the tile, requires the cord to stay clear of it, and puts the 36 endpoint there. That keeps 36, 46 and the machine in three separate regions.

I did not widen or invent geometry to accommodate the renderer. The perimeter member standing proud of the second side with a visible outer surface is the disclosed loop or skirt; only its drawn depth is declared a schematic convention, and that declaration stays inside the figure brief, never reaching the text or claims.

Adding explicit hatch directions and the strip descriptions pushed three briefs over the character limit, so I trimmed duplicated wording rather than required geometry: in FIG. 4 the naming of the three bands is merged into the hatching sentence instead of being stated twice; in FIG. 5 the omission of the motor and extraction mechanism is stated once in the view line rather than repeated in the device bullet. Final lengths are 2789, 2792, 2031, 2792 and 2765.

I also confirmed the earlier text repairs survived this cycle: the FIG. 5 sentence in the Brief Description still recites the flexible pulling element and its connection as shown schematically, the description still says the second side 16 is opposite the first side 14, and all five paragraphs of the Brief Description carry their schematic declarations.
changes: figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md: replaced the abstract different-angle requirement with explicit hatch directions, base 12 rising to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs of perimeter member 24 falling to the right at about 45 degrees, covering element 36 rising to the right at a shallow slope, prefaced by the statement that touching bodies never share a hatching direction.

figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: each body now carries a stated hatch direction, covering element 36 rising at about 45 degrees, bonding material 40 falling at about 45 degrees, substrate 42 rising shallowly and the column falling shallowly; band naming merged into that sentence to keep the brief within length.

figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md: the band's front surface is specified as a broad strip between the underside of the slab and the tile, its depth declared schematic; numeral 24 is now identified well inside that strip, clear of both boundaries.

figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: the ring band is required to be drawn broad with its outer and inner edges well apart; numeral 24 is identified inside the band on the straight left-hand side of the ring, clear of both edges and not in the enclosed open field.

figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: added the open stretch of tile in front of the machine, required the flexible pulling element to stay clear of it, moved numeral 36 there, and specified the band's broad front strip with numeral 24 inside it clear of both boundaries.
figures/FIG-1-...md and figures/FIG-5-...md: condensed duplicated wording in the handle bullet and the device bullet respectively so both briefs stay within the 2800-character limit.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged; this turn touched only figure briefs, and hatch angles and drawn depths are depiction conventions that add no technical matter. Claim 1 still rests on the combination no reference in prior_art/ discloses: a rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately does not seal, leaving a clearance along at least part of its length through which ambient air enters continuously; an extraction rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the differential is maintained. The rigid, seal-free perimeter carries the claim clear of US-11408462-B2 and DE-202021002652-U1, which both place a compliant member, elastic partitions or a rubber-elastic apron, in the load path. Simultaneous holding and sliding under one continuously running extraction carries it clear of US-10001245-B2, which surrenders the vacuum and floats on an air cushion to move. The non-sealing clearance, and vibration delivered into the covering element as the working output rather than spent loosening the hold, carry it clear of US-4934475-A. US-11247858-B2 is addressed in the Background for the teaching it actually contains, lifting sheet articles on a perforated suction plate and sweeping debris by suction, and why that does not bear on holding a vibrating tool down on a laid covering element.

content.content:
1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Full ledger traced. Every claim limitation (claims 1–18), every one of the 16 numbered parts, and every structure, relationship, material, result, operating condition and variant in the Field, Summary, Detailed Description and the five figure briefs traces to an exact affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md (the sole USER disclosure, repeated verbatim as the first USER turn in input/conversation.md). Specifically: rigid base with first/second sides, motor on the first side, air-extraction mechanism (vacuum pump) on the first side in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side, rigid low-friction perimeter loop/skirt of plastic/metal/PTFE/combination of rigid materials, non-sealing perimeter that restricts but does not stop inflow, air entering beneath the perimeter (the "clearance 34"), continuous extraction maintaining sub-atmospheric chamber pressure, pressure differential holding the device down without operator pressure, all-rigid transmission path with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup, sliding to successive areas while the vacuum maintains contact, one or more guiding handles, and the rope/wire/cable pulling element with decoupled control - all appear affirmatively in the disclosure. Later USER turns are operational/corrective QA only and were not used as support; the earlier list of unsupported features (PTFE facing, through-base duct, support column, exhaust, no-valve limitation, power source, integral loop, attachment formation, plural chambers, vertical-surface use, bail geometry) has in fact been removed from the current text, numerals and briefs. Internal consistency checks pass: claim and description terminology are identical; each numeral means one thing and every numeral in the table appears both in the text and on exactly the sheets its brief lists (union of the five sheets = all 16 numerals, max 7 per sheet); the Brief Description of the Drawings matches every figure brief in view type, omissions and schematic disclaimers; the FIG. 2 (contact) versus FIG. 4 (clearance) section locations are expressly reconciled in the description; claim dependencies (1, 10, 14 independent; 18 total) and antecedent bases are sound; the abstract is 149 words; and no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction to a person, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains anywhere in draft/ or figures/. The rectangular slab/ring outlines, the closed-ring grip, the plain housings and the loose-cord path are permissible depiction conventions: each is declared "shown schematically"/"a depiction convention for this sheet only" in its brief and mirrored in the Brief Description, the claims and description stay shape-neutral, no exact proportion or count is asserted (each brief expressly disclaims proportion), and no application sentence adds an "by way of example" or "any closed outline" embodiment to justify a renderer's choice. One elaboration in the Detailed Description exceeds its source and is reported below.
4	
5	## Mechanical checks that did not pass

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
